title: Climbing Stairs
prompt:
A staircase has n steps. Each move you climb either 1 step or 2 steps. In how many different ways can you reach the top?

Write climbStairs(n).

climbStairs(2);  // 2   (1+1, 2)
climbStairs(3);  // 3   (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1)
climbStairs(5);  // 8

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 70. (The answer for 70 is about 3 × 1014, which still fits exactly in a JavaScript number.)

Warning: the plain recursive version is correct but makes about 2 × 3 × 1014 calls for n = 70, so the last test first times n = 35 and stops with a hint if your solution is exponential. Starting with plain recursion is fine: watch that test fail, then add memoization.

tests.name: one step has exactly one way
n = 70 (needs memoization or a table)

hints: Trigger: "how many different ways" plus a choice at each step (1 or 2). Counting ways where the same sub-question repeats is DP.

Idea: think about the last move. To stand on step n, you came from step n-1 (then took 1) or from step n-2 (then took 2). So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2. Plain recursion recomputes the same ways(k) millions of times; a Map memo computes each once.

Code shape (memo): const memo = new Map(); function ways(k) { if (k <= 2) return k; if (memo.has(k)) return memo.get(k); const r = ways(k - 1) + ways(k - 2); memo.set(k, r); return r; }. Code shape (table): loop from 3 to n keeping only the last two values.
explain:
Time O(n): each step is computed once. Space O(1) for the two-variable table (O(n) with a memo or a full array). Plain recursion was O(2n) because the same subproblems were solved again and again.

Say it: "The number of ways to reach step n is the ways to reach n minus 1 plus the ways to reach n minus 2, because the last move is a 1 or a 2. The plain recursion repeats subproblems, so I memoize, then turn it into a bottom-up loop that only keeps the last two values: O(n) time, O(1) space." Yes, these are the Fibonacci numbers.
